Infinitives of Purpose in Tenses with Simple Present.
We can use the infinitives of verbs to show the objective of something what we are doing.
But scientist and scholars, centuries ago, used the term data to refer to a given fact in the world.
Those tools establish the context of the data, making data meaningful for humans to interpret data.
It is not the system the one that decides what grade to deserve, it is the human who programs the system to do so.

The preposition to before a verb indicates its infinitive form, which is used to express the reason we have for doing something. We can use it at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence.


Examples:
To improve the system, we need a new software developer.
I check the system in the morning, to make sure there are no viruses.

Remember that the verb with to is the one that shows the purpose of the actions.

Examples:
I work on my software program every day to finish it on time.

Notice that when the preposition to is in the middle of the sentence, we do not use a comma to split the sentences.

To talk about the purpose of a habit or a routine we express our goals with the preposition to + infinitive, and we use the simple present to show the actions taken to achieve our purpose.

Contrast, Simple Present and Present Continuous to Talk about Permanent States, and Current Actions.
We use both the present simple and the present continuous to talk about the present, but both structures have completely different meanings and uses.
I'm reading a great book about systems engineering, you know I'm very fond of reading.
I usually read an online magazine about systems on bBlog, and the article I'm reading at the moment is about data.
I work in computer science, and I'm learning how to understand data through different programming languages

Simple present is a tense used to talk about permanent situations in the present, general facts and trues that are not likely to change.

Examples:
We work at a big multinational.
I know about information systems.

The simple present has a very simple structure in its affirmative form. But, there is only one important fact you need to remember, when you talk indirectly about one single person or object (third person singular form; he, she and it) you add an -s or an -es to the verb.

Example:
I work with software programs.
He knows a lot about computers.

On the other hand, we use the present continuous tense to talk about temporary situations and about things that are happening at the moment of speaking (or just for a certain period of time) but are going to change in the future.

Examples: This year we’re living in Bogotá.
I’m studying about information systems at the moment.

Notice that the present continuous is usually accompanied by temporary time expressions such as at the moment, this week, now or right now.

Do not forget to use the verb to be conjugated when you are making a present continuous sentence.

Examples:
Now I am working at a systems company.  
We are repairing systems at a café at the moment.

There are some verbs in English we don’t use in the present continuous, even if we are talking about a situation happening at the moment of speaking. Those verbs are the ones related to emotions (like, hate), the ones connected to mental functions (think, remember), the verb have, when talking about possessions, and the verb need. These verbs are called stative verbs.

List of Programming and Computer Science Words
There are thousands of words and expressions related to computer science and programming that you probably already know. Here we are going to revise some of them.
I usually read an online magazine about systems on bBlog, and the article I'm reading at the moment is about data.

These are some terms and programs we use when working on the computer science field:

  • B2evolution: is a content and community management system supported by a MySQL database. It has GNU public license.

  • Backup: to copy data, information and others on an extra media, apart from its original. .

  • Baitware: refers to defective software with limited defects, offered for free in order to attract users to commercial products. .

  • bBlog: is a publishing and content system manager used to manage frequently updated information specially from weblogs. It also has a GNU public license.

  • Bedroom Programming: is a practice which consist of one or a group of amateur programmers developing software (especially computer games) with no intention of making a profit, but just because they love it.

Johanna: Hey, Tom! I'm reading a great book about systems engineering, you know I'm very fond of reading.
Tom: Yes, I know. What's the article about?
Johanna: It's about the concept of data. Nowadays, we relate data to computing and systems, but centuries ago, scientists and scholars used the term data to refer to a given fact in the world; for instance, a notch in a stick. When we talk about information stored in computers or any digital media, data is a representation of facts from reality. They are characterized as binary states, which are bit patterns with no meaning or sense.

Tom: Oh, I heard about that. I usually read an online magazine about systems on bBlog, and the article I'm reading at the moment is about data. They say that data doesn't have meaning by itself, but it needs to be translated by a programming language and defined by data statements. Those tools establish the context of the data, making data meaningful for humans to interpret it. Human beings are the only ones capable of making sense of the data and context. But, what is the use of data in real life?

Johanna: Well, data has lots of important usages. For example, in the educational field, software defines a grade as good or bad, as a result of the purpose and interpretation of the test designer. It is not the system the one that decides what grade to deserve, it is the human who programs the system to do so.
I work in computer science, and I'm learning how to understand data through different programming languages; data binary states can be interpreted as letters, numbers, parts of numbers, and so forth. So in the banking field, for instance, data may be translated into clients' codes and figures
Tom: That's very fascinating, isn't it?
